title: Separable fields are geometrically normal
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and $K/k$ a separable field extension [def-pc-field-extension, def-weil-pbc-separable-field-extension], meaning that every finitely generated subextension is separably generated. Then $K$ is geometrically normal over $k$: for every field extension $E/k$, the commutative tensor-product algebra $K\otimes_k E$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] is a normal ring [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring], meaning that each prime localization is an integrally closed domain. No algebraicity or finite generation of either field extension is assumed.

proof.text: Choose a perfect purely inseparable overfield $P/k$ by [lem-weil-pbc-perfect-purely-inseparable-overfield], and put $R=K\otimes_k P$. Write $q=1$ in characteristic zero and $q=p$ in characteristic $p>0$ as in that node. The hypotheses on $P$ identify a perfect closure; no finite-degree assumption is made.

We first prove $R$ reduced, spelling out the separable (rather than separably generated) case of 030U. Let $z\in R$ satisfy $z^m=0$ with $m>0$. Write $z=\sum_{i=1}^r a_i\otimes b_i$; finite tensor expressions follow from [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. The field $F=k(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\subseteq K$ is finitely generated, hence separably generated by [def-weil-pbc-separable-field-extension] and the hypothesis. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-separably-generated-tensor-reduced] with the reduced algebra $P$ (if a nonzero element of a field had zero positive power, multiplying by its inverse power would give $1=0$) to get $F\otimes_k P$ reduced. Since $P$ is flat over $k$ by [lem-weil-pbc-module-over-field-flat], the definition [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map] says tensoring the inclusion $F\hookrightarrow K$ with $P$ is injective. Lift $z$ to $z_F=\sum_i a_i\otimes b_i$ in $F\otimes_k P$. Injectivity gives $z_F^m=0$, reducedness gives $z_F=0$, and therefore $z=0$.

proof.text: For every $z=\sum_i a_i\otimes b_i\in R$ there is $n\ge0$ such that $z^{q^n}$ is in the image of $K\to R$, $a\mapsto a\otimes1$. Indeed choose $n$ at least all exponents for the finitely many $b_i$ given by step 1; if $b_i^{p^{n_i}}\in k$ and $n\ge n_i$, then $b_i^{p^n}=(b_i^{p^{n_i}})^{p^{n-n_i}}\in k$. In characteristic $p$, repeated Frobenius additivity yields $z^{p^n}=\sum_i a_i^{p^n}\otimes b_i^{p^n}=(\sum_i a_i^{p^n}b_i^{p^n})\otimes1$, since each $b_i^{p^n}\in k$. Frobenius additivity is the binomial formula: for $0<j<p$, $p\mid\binom pj$, so all mixed terms vanish; iterate this identity. In characteristic zero $q=1$ and the power condition forces every $b_i\in k$, so the same assertion holds with $n=0$.

proof.text: A field has only the zero prime, its localization at that prime is itself, and its fraction field is itself. Therefore $R$ is normal by [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. By [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], the bilinear swap induces a linear map; the multiplication formula on pure tensors shows it is a ring map. Use the swap map $a\otimes b\mapsto b\otimes a$, whose inverse is the same formula, to identify $R$ with $P\otimes_k K$. Apply (1) implies (2) of [lem-weil-pbc-geometrically-normal-perfect-closure-criterion] to $A=K$ and the perfect purely inseparable $P$ of step 1. It gives normality of $E\otimes_k K$ for every $E/k$. The same tensor swap gives the required normality of $K\otimes_k E$. Normality is invariant under a ring isomorphism because it bijects prime ideals and induces isomorphisms of their localizations and fraction fields, preserving monic equations.
